contents.name: Contents: 10. Cayley-Hamilton Theorem and 14. Krull-Cohen-Seidenberg Theory
Definition (10.21), module-finite algebras and elements integral over the base ring
Proposition (10.23), one-element integral dependence via finite modules
Exercise (10.24), an explicit quadratic equation over k[X^2] for an element of k[X]
Theorem (10.28), finitely generated integral algebras are module-finite
Theorem (10.28), module-finite algebras are integral
contents.reason: The page reuses the already-published one-element criterion together with the finite-generator lemma instead of minting a second global finite-type equivalence theorem whose only new clause would duplicate that older abstract-algebra result.

contents.name: Exercise (10.31)(1), products preserve integrality componentwise
contents.reason: This page stays on one extension and its prime-spectrum behavior. Product decompositions and componentwise normalization are not used by the Cohen-Seidenberg proofs or the chosen examples.

contents.name: Exercise (10.31)(2), products preserve being integrally closed componentwise
contents.reason: The companion page uses the cusp subring only inside the lying-over example, and the A-page proof route never needs a separate product-normality theorem here.

contents.name: Theorem (10.32), the integral closure is an algebra and is integrally closed
Example (10.34)(2), Z[(1+sqrt(5))/2] is the normalization of Z[sqrt(5)]
contents.reason: This is a good arithmetic normalization example, but the batch already keeps one finite-module quadratic computation and one explicit going-down counterexample. A second normalization computation would duplicate the same seam without supporting a later proof on this page.

contents.name: Example (10.34)(3), the quadratic-order normalization Z + Z delta inside Q(sqrt(d))
contents.reason: The example is mathematically valid, but the companion page keeps its quadratic arithmetic on a two-generator finite module instead of opening a second normalization branch with order-specific notation.

contents.name: Example (10.34)(4), the integral closure of k[t^2, t^3] in k(t) is k[t]
contents.reason: The cusp ring still appears in the lying-over example, but the companion page's final slot is now spent on the missing source-backed counterexample showing that going down can fail when the base is not normal. A separate normalization computation of the same cusp ring would duplicate that seam.

contents.name: Lemma (14.1), an integral extension of domains is a field upstairs if and only if it is a field downstairs
Definition (14.2), a prime upstairs lies over its contraction downstairs
Theorem (14.3)(1), maximality is preserved under lying over
Theorem (14.3)(2), incomparable over-primes cannot be nested
Exercise (14.4)(a)-(c), the local ring over a unique over-prime and its integrality over the base localisation
Exercise (14.5), a second over-prime makes the upper prime-localisation nonintegral over the lower one
contents.reason: The page already states incomparability directly and keeps the companion localisation example on clearing denominators rather than on the distinct-over-primes obstruction to integrality of one chosen prime localisation.

contents.name: Exercise (14.6), the localised quadratic example with Y = X^2
Lemma (14.7), monic factors of a monic polynomial have integral coefficients
Proposition (14.8), minimal polynomials over the fraction field of a normal domain have coefficients in the domain
Theorem (14.9), going down for integral extensions
Lemma (14.10), minimal primes consist of zero divisors
contents.reason: This zero-divisor theorem already belongs to the published associated-prime and support pages. The current page uses it only as source background inside the flatness proof, which is itself kept out of scope.

contents.name: Theorem (14.11), going down for flat algebras
contents.reason: The design for this page fixes the going-down route through integral extensions over normal domains. Flat going-down belongs to the later flatness and dimension interfaces rather than to this Cohen-Seidenberg page.

sources.title: J. S. Milne, A Primer of Commutative Algebra, v4.03 (March 23, 2020)

contents.name: Corollary 6.3
contents.reason: The two directions this corollary packages are already split across earlier published items, and the page does not need a separate named finite-versus-integral equivalence theorem beyond those components.

contents.name: Corollary 6.8
contents.reason: The field-of-fractions reconstruction of the integral closure is useful background, but the current page does not need it as a separate item for the chosen proofs or examples.

contents.name: Proposition 6.10
contents.reason: Normality of unique factorization domains is a valid application, but this page does not open a separate UFD branch. The later normalisation and Dedekind-domain pages are the natural home for that example.

contents.name: Remark 7.2
contents.reason: The unit-intersection identity is true and useful, but no proof on this page needs it as a separate named result once the field criterion itself is retained.

contents.name: Aside 7.8
contents.reason: This is a failure example for a nonintegral extension, whereas the companion page is kept on sourced examples inside the integral-extension and normalization route that the A page actually proves.
